question: At the end of life, cells struggle to produce enough of which main energy molecule?
explanation: Cells need adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to power their everyday work. When oxygen drops at the end of life, ATP production stops too. You've got this! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why do body cells swell and break open during the final stages of dying?

options.A: Sodium and water rush in because cell pumps stop working
options.B: Lactic acid builds up inside blood vessels
options.C: White blood cells attack healthy tissues
options.D: Extra glucose pulls water into the cells

explanation: Without ATP, the tiny pumps that keep sodium out of cells stop working. Sodium stays inside, brings water with it, and causes the cell to swell. Great thinking! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h1)

question: What is the medical term for the patchy, purplish skin color that appears on the hands and feet when circulation slows down?
explanation: Mottling happens when blood flow slows way down, causing blood to pool in the hands and feet with a purplish, blotchy pattern. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h2)

question: You cannot feel a dying patient's radial pulse at the wrist. What should you do next as the nurse?

options.A: Call the doctor immediately to start IV fluids
options.B: Apply a warm water bottle to their hands
options.C: Pump the blood pressure cuff higher on their arm
options.D: Check a central pulse like the carotid or femoral

explanation: When peripheral circulation gets weak, wrist pulses fade first. Checking a central pulse helps you accurately check the remaining heart activity. You're building great clinical instincts! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h2)

question: What actually causes the noisy breathing known as the 'death rattle' in a dying patient?

options.A: Air moving past pooled saliva and mucus in the upper airway
options.B: Spasms of the chest diaphragm muscle
options.C: Narrowing of the main windpipe from inflammation
options.D: Fluid filling up the small air sacs deep in the lungs

explanation: The death rattle sounds scary, but it's just air passing over saliva that the patient is too weak to cough up or swallow. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which breathing pattern features deep, fast breaths followed by a temporary pause in breathing?
explanation: Cheyne-Stokes breathing has regular cycles of breaths getting deeper and faster, then slowing down into a short pause (apnea). It's very common near the end of life. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which human sense is widely believed to be the absolute last to fade before a patient dies?
explanation: Hearing usually stays intact longer than other senses. That's why we always encourage families to keep talking and comforting their loved ones right up until the end. Beautiful nursing knowledge! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why might a dying patient suddenly become restless, pull at their blankets, or reach into the air?

options.A: Brain changes and internal discomfort can cause terminal delirium
options.B: The patient is experiencing a burst of physical strength
options.C: High oxygen levels in the brain are causing extra activity
options.D: Normal vision is suddenly returning before death

explanation: Terminal delirium is a normal reaction to organ changes, toxin buildup, or hidden discomfort like a full bladder. Identifying this helps us keep the patient peaceful. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the medical term for when the kidneys stop producing urine altogether at the end of life?
explanation: Anuria means complete lack of urine production because blood flow to the kidneys has slowed to a stop. You're mastering your medical terms! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h5)

question: How should you as a nurse view a dying patient's refusal to eat and drink?

options.A: As an urgent sign to start artificial tube feeding right away
options.B: As a normal part of the body shutting down its digestive functions
options.C: As a psychological sign of severe hopelessness
options.D: As a sign that the patient has a blocked bowel

explanation: The digestive system naturally slows down at the end of life. Forcing food or water can actually cause nausea and discomfort. Trust your training! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h5)

question: What common facial feature is often seen during the active dying phase because muscles completely relax?
explanation: When facial muscles lose all their tone, the jaw naturally sags open during the active dying phase. Every clinical detail you learn makes you a better nurse! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing care once a patient enters the active dying phase?

options.A: Checking blood pressure and pulse every fifteen minutes
options.B: Trying to restart vital signs with emergency medications
options.C: Ensuring absolute comfort and supporting the family
options.D: Forcing fluids by mouth to stop dehydration

explanation: When active dying begins, our focus shifts completely from trying to cure to keeping the patient comfortable and wrapping the family in support. You are doing amazing! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T4#GNS221_U4_T4_h6)
